New Study Suggests Humans Lived in North America 130,000 Years Ago

Yes, yes, I know NPR is not a reputable source, but the journal Nature sure is; and the abstract, found here, is nothing short of astounding.

In summary:

In 1992, archaeologists working a highway construction site in San Diego County found the partial skeleton of a mastodon. That isn't unusual in itself, but this particular skeleton was. "The remains were in association with a number of sharply broken rocks and broken bones," says Tom Demere, paleontologist at the San Diego Natural History Museum and author of the paper. He says the rocks showed clear marks of having been used as hammers and an anvil. And some of the bones, as well as a tooth, showed fractures characteristic of being hammered, apparently with those same stones. It looked like the work of humans. Yet there were no cut marks on the bones showing that the animal was butchered for meat. "The suggestion is that this site is strictly for breaking bone," Demere says, "to produce blank material, raw material to make bone tools or to extract marrow."

But new evidence about this find, made possible by using new uranium-thorium dating technology which didn't exist when the bones were first uncovered, is jaw-dropping.

The bones are 130,000 years old.

From the abstract:

The CM site is, to our knowledge, the oldest in situ, well-documented archaeological site in North America and, as such, substantially revises the timing of arrival of Homo into the Americas.

If I may briefly offer my own thoughts as well, the find also shows that early humans--far from being stupid cavemen as they are characterized in popular culture--possessed a remarkable degree of sophistication. It not only demonstrates that human beings inhabited the Americas far earlier than we previously thought, it demonstrates that they were far smarter than we give them credit for.
